steps.body:
P(roll a 6) = 1/6. Now someone tells you the roll came up **even**. The three odd faces are gone — they were never possible after all — and the 6 is one of the three faces still standing.

Information does not change the die. It changes the **set of outcomes you are choosing among**.

widget.prompt: Three outcomes remain. Shade the ones that are a 6 — that fraction is P(6 | even).
widget.successFeedback: 1 of the 3 surviving outcomes is a 6, so P(6 | even) = 1/3. The condition doubled the probability by shrinking the denominator.
widget.lowFeedback: Shade the 6. It is still possible — being even is exactly what a 6 is.
widget.highFeedback: Only one of the three even faces is a 6. The 2 and the 4 are even but are not sixes.

predict.prompt: You'll shade 1/3 of the grid. Will that cover more or less than half of it?
predict.reveal: Half means the numerator is half the denominator — 1.5/3 here — and 1 is less. Probability as shaded area makes the benchmark visible before you count a single cell.

cml.actionGoal: Select regions of an equal-outcome sample space and coordinate area with event probability.

explanationVariants: The numerator is still one outcome — the 6. The denominator fell from 6 possible faces to the 3 even ones, so the probability rose from 1/6 to 1/3.
Conditioning throws away outcomes that contradict what you were told. Here it deletes 1, 3 and 5, leaving a smaller world to divide by.

widget.prompt: Being told "the roll is even" raises P(6) from 1/6 to 1/3. Why?

options.label: The set of possible outcomes shrank from 6 to 3, while the 6 is still one outcome.
options.feedback: Right — same numerator, smaller denominator, bigger fraction.

options.label: The die became more likely to land on 6.
options.feedback: The die is unchanged and was never influenced by what you were told. Only your set of live possibilities shrank.

options.label: There are now 2 sixes among the even faces.
options.feedback: There is still exactly one 6 on a die. The numerator stayed at 1 — it is the denominator that moved.

options.label: Because 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3.
options.feedback: That arithmetic is a coincidence here. The real move is 1 favourable outcome out of 3 survivors.

explanationVariants: Once you know it is a face card, only 12 cards remain, and 4 of them are kings: 4/12 ≈ 0.333.

widget.prompt: A card is drawn. You are told it is a **face card** (J, Q or K). Find P(king | face card) as a decimal, to three places.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 4/52 — the unconditional P(king). It ignores what you were told, which was supposed to shrink the deck to 12 cards.
That is 12/52 = P(face card) — the condition itself, not the probability of a king inside it.
That is 1/4, which would be right if there were 4 equally likely face-card ranks. There are only 3 (J, Q, K), so the kings are 4 of 12.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Only 12 cards are still possible, and 4 are kings: 4/12 ≈ 0.333.

steps.body:
Written as a formula:

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B).

Read it as: *of the B-world, how much is also A?* The numerator must be the part of A **inside** B — an outcome outside B is no longer on the table. Both parts are measured against the same original total, so that total cancels.

explanationVariants: B occupies 40% of the world and A∩B occupies 12%. So A takes up 12/40 = 30% of B.

widget.prompt: P(A ∩ B) = 0.12 and P(B) = 0.40. Find P(A | B).

commonErrors.feedback: That is 0.12 × 0.40. Conditioning divides by P(B) — multiplying by it would make the answer smaller, but knowing B happened cannot shrink A's share of B.
That is 0.40/1.2 or a guess at 1/3. The formula puts the intersection on top and the condition underneath: 0.12/0.40.
That is 0.12 + 0.40. Adding an intersection to a whole event double-counts and answers nothing — conditioning is a ratio, not a sum.

explanationVariants: Told the card is a heart, the world is the 13 hearts. Exactly one of them is the king of hearts: 1/13.

widget.prompt: You are told the card is a **heart**. What is P(king | heart)?

options.feedback: Right — 13 hearts remain and exactly one is a king.
That is the unconditional P(king). Three of those four kings are not hearts, so they were ruled out the moment you were told the suit.
That keeps all four kings but shrinks the deck to hearts — mixing the two worlds. Only the king of hearts survives the condition.
That is P(heart), the condition itself. You want the kings inside that group.

hints: First list the rolls of two dice whose total is more than 9. Order matters: (4,6) and (6,4) are different rolls.
They are (4,6), (6,4), (5,5), (5,6), (6,5), (6,6) — six rolls in all. That six is your new denominator.
Now count the doubles among those six, and divide.
explanationVariants: Six rolls total more than 9. Two of them — (5,5) and (6,6) — are doubles, so P(double | sum > 9) = 2/6 ≈ 0.333.
P(double and sum>9)/P(sum>9) = (2/36)/(6/36) = 2/6 = 1/3. The 36 cancels, which is why you can just count inside the condition.

widget.prompt: Two dice are rolled and you are told the total is **more than 9**. Find P(the roll is a double), to three places.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 2/36 — the unconditional chance of rolling (5,5) or (6,6) out of all 36 rolls. The condition was meant to cut the 36 down to 6.
That is 6/36 = P(sum > 9) — the condition itself, which belongs underneath the fraction, not in front of it.
That is 4/6, the chance the roll is **not** a double given the sum is over 9. It is the complement of the answer.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Six rolls beat 9; two of them are doubles: 2/6 ≈ 0.333.

steps.body: Conditioning is a change of denominator.
takeaways: Being told B happened deletes every outcome outside B. What survives is your new world.
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) — the part of A inside B, over all of B.
The numerator can only shrink or stay the same, but the denominator shrinks too, so a conditional probability can go up or down.
steps.teaser: Next: the same 40 students, two different conditionals — and the error that swaps them.

concept.body: When you are told B happened, cross out every outcome where B is false. Then just count: how many of the survivors are also A? That count over the number of survivors **is** the conditional probability.

explanationVariants: Odd faces are 1, 3, 5 — three survivors. Two of them (3 and 5) are greater than 2, so 2/3.

widget.prompt: A die is rolled and you are told the result is **odd**. How many of the surviving outcomes are greater than 2?

commonErrors.feedback: All three survivors are odd, but only 3 and 5 clear the bar of 'greater than 2' — the 1 does not.
That counts 3, 4, 5 and 6 from the full die. The even faces were ruled out by the condition, so 4 and 6 are gone.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Survivors: 1, 3, 5. Greater than 2: 3 and 5. That is 2 of 3.
